title: How Ping Pong Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of ping pong (table tennis). They cover its probable British origins with improvised equipment (cigar box lids, a whittled cork), early names like Gossima and the trademarking of "ping pong" in 1901, the switch to celluloid balls, the dimpled rubber paddle covering, and the rise and fall of the sport in the early twentieth century. They discuss the jazz-age boom, the early world championships dominated by Hungary and Europe, Hiroji Sato's foam paddle at the 1952 Worlds, rule changes such as smaller net, bigger ball, and Olympic status, and a famous 1930s-era story of a two-hour-twelve-minute zero-zero point between Erlick and Farcas that the hosts doubt. They also cover ball manufacturing and testing, paddle grips and spin, the Magnus effect, cheating with glued foam, ping pong diplomacy between the US and China in 1971, table tennis robots such as Forpheus, and a listener email correcting the hosts on life expectancy.

segments.title: Opening banter and ping pong fandom
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about playing ping pong at home and introduce the topic, noting table tennis is a racket sport that is popular worldwide.

segments.title: British origins and early names
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the British invention of table tennis from improvised tabletop tennis with cigar box lids and a cork, early names such as Gossima, and the trademarking of ping pong in 1901 by Jaques and Son and Parker Brothers. They also cover James Debenham's failed patent attempt in 1885.

segments.title: Celluloid balls and the rubber paddle covering
segments.summary: James Gibb's celluloid ball made ping pong playable, and a dimpled rubber covering wrapped around the paddle by a player improved spin, setting the stage for the sport's growth.

segments.title: Fad decline, jazz age boom, and early world championships
segments.summary: Ping pong faded after its early popularity, possibly tied to a 1914 National Guard remark about ping pong warriors and to World War One and the Spanish flu. It returned in the jazz age with Parker Brothers tournaments, and the ITTF was formed and held world championships starting in 1926. Hungary and Europe dominated early, with Victor Barna winning several titles.

segments.title: Hiroji Sato and the foam paddle
segments.summary: At the 1952 World Championship, Hiroji Sato used a foam-covered paddle to win, a move that was controversial in Japan and which he did not follow with further tournament play. The hosts also note the US lagged behind and that the sport was Olympic later.

segments.title: Erlick and Farcas zero-zero match legend
segments.summary: The hosts recount a story, reported in Sports Illustrated, of a legendary chiseler match between Alex Erlick and Penneth Farcas in which the first point reportedly lasted two hours and twelve minutes. They express doubt about the embellished details, and discuss Erlick's survival of the Holocaust and return to table tennis.

segments.title: Rules, equipment manufacturing, and playing styles
segments.summary: The hosts cover rule changes such as lowering the net, enlarging the ball in 2000, and scoring to eleven in competition. They describe how balls are made and tested, paddle construction and sides, and grips such as shakehand, penhold, and the Seemiller grip. They explain spin, the Magnus effect, and loop shots, and mention house rules and foam glue cheating.

segments.title: Ping pong diplomacy and table tennis robots
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1971 ping pong diplomacy in which the US team visited China after Glenn Cowan's bus encounter with the Chinese team, which helped thaw relations before Nixon's trip. They also discuss table tennis robots, including Forpheus, and a speed record of 173 hits in 60 seconds.

segments.title: Listener mail on life expectancy and figs and dates
segments.summary: A listener, Joseph Catrell, corrects the hosts on average life expectancy versus infant and childhood mortality. The hosts also acknowledge an earlier error equating figs and dates.
